paragraphs: Shmuel the priest: Megillah 22, end of side a. The son of Abba bar Abba; see his entry.

1. (a) (a) He was called Yarhinai because he was versed in the secret of intercalation, and the paths of heaven were as clear to him as the paths of Nehardea, his home. In Tosafot, Bava Batra 7, beginning of side b: “Shmuel too was a Nehardean.” He said that he could arrange the calendar for the entire Diaspora without witnesses' sightings. Abba, the father of R' Simlai, said to him, “Does the master know …?” He answered, “No.” He said to him, “Since the master does not know this, there are other matters that he does not know”: Rosh Hashanah 20b. At the end of Shabbat, Ablat—he was a gentile—was a great scholar of astronomy, his colleague. (It is puzzling that he calls him his colleague.) He was a great physician and healed Rabbi. Rabbi wished to ordain him but did not succeed. Shmuel told him not to distress himself: he had seen the book of Adam the first man, in which it was written, “Shmuel Yarhinai shall be called a sage; he shall not be called Rabbi, and Rabbi's healing shall be through him”: Bava Metzia 85b. Perhaps he descended from Eli and therefore was not ordained, as in the first chapter of Sanhedrin, 14a: “There shall not be an elder in your house”—this refers to ordination. In the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Af al Pi, halakhah 6: he recognized the midwife who delivered him.

(b) He was called Mar Shmuel in Shabbat 108, end of side b, and Kiddushin 21b. R' Mattana said, “I came before Mar Shmuel”: Sukkah 11b; also Hullin 105, end of side a. There, 111, end of side b: R' Elazar was attending Mar Shmuel. Fish that had been placed in a bowl were brought before him, and he ate them with kutah. He offered him some, but he did not eat. He said to him, “I gave some to your teacher, and he ate.” He came before Rav and asked, “Has the master retracted his teaching?” He answered, “Far be it from the offspring of Abba bar Abba to feed me something that I do not hold permissible.” See responsa Ralbah, no. 121; responsa Rashdam; and Be'er Sheva, 84, 85, which explain this: how did Shmuel utter a falsehood in order to feed R' Elazar something forbidden in his view? And why did R' Elazar not eat—did he not believe Shmuel that Rav had eaten?

(c) He was called Shakud: Ketubbot 43b; Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Na'arah she-Nitpattatah, halakhah 2.

(d) He was called Aryokh. At the beginning of Ha-Tekhelet, 38b, Levi said to Shmuel, “Aryokh, do not sit down on your feet until you explain it to me.” Rashi explains Aryokh as an expression for a king, as in “Yehudah is a lion's cub.” He calls him Aryokh because we hold that the halakhah follows Shmuel in civil law, just as “the law of the kingdom is law.” In Shabbat, Rashi explains that it is because he was expert in civil law and judged like a king; it is an expression related to rikha. Tosafot write that Aryokh is a king's name, “Aryokh king of Ellasar.” This king rather than the other kings was chosen because the word ari, “lion,” is embedded in his name. From this you can see how to correct an error in Yalkut Reuveni, Lekh Lekha. In Hullin 76b, Rashi explains: after Aryokh king of Ellasar, because the halakhah follows him in civil law—a king, el sar, excluding matters of prohibition and permission, in which the halakhah follows Rav. Tosafot, Shabbat 53, write likewise; that is, el issur, excluding prohibition. It seems to me to be along the lines of “A king establishes the land through justice”: if the judge resembles a king who needs nothing. Rashi explains that he is wealthy; Tosafot explain that he is expert in the laws and need not ask others. Because he was expert in the laws, they called him Aryokh, an expression related to rikha.

The Arukh ha-Katzar writes that he was called Aryokh because he was a physician, from “I shall bring healing [arukhah] to you.” I did not find this. Rather, its wording is: “Arakh: in the first chapter of Kelim, la'alot arukhah, an expression for healing.” It did not write this—that he was called Aryokh because he was a physician. “Some say it is because the lion is king of the beasts; others say he was tall.” End of quotation. I say that this is not so, for he was short. (In Nedarim 50b, “Shmuel was a short man”—gloss.) Perhaps it is a euphemistic opposite, like “abundant light” for blindness: Yuhasin, under aleph.

(e) He was called Shapur Malka. Bava Kamma 96b: Rav Nahman said, “Huna our colleague said concerning me, ‘I and Shapur Malka’”—meaning Shmuel—“‘are brothers in civil law.’” At the end of Bava Metzia, Resh Lakish said, “The halakhah follows R' Shimon.” They said this before Shapur Malka, who told them, “Let our commendation reach R' Shimon.” Rashi explains: it appears to mean the actual Shapur Malka, a king who was expert in the laws. Tosafot write: as at the end of Avodah Zarah, when he cut the citron for Rav Yehudah, he thrust the knife ten times into hard earth. Some say that Shapur Malka means Shmuel, since he is called this in several places, but this does not fit the passage well. Yuhasin writes that the initials of “Shmuel” are “Shapur Malka”: like the king of Persia, he was expert in the laws. It does not seem right to make his expertise depend on the king of Persia. Was there no expert in the laws among Israel to whom it could be related? Moreover, the halakhah follows Shmuel in civil law, not in prohibitions, whereas the Persian king's expertise concerned a prohibition, the knife, and so forth.

In Pesahim 54, end of side a, Rava said, “I shall say something that Shapur Malka did not say.” Who is that? Shmuel. Rashi explains: Rava calls Shmuel Shapur Malka because he was expert in civil law, and the halakhah follows him in civil law, like a judgment issued by a king, which stands. Shapur Malka was a king of the Persians in Rava's time. End of quotation. It seems to me that he was called Shapur Malka because he was esteemed by the king of Persia. Thus in Sukkah 53a, Shmuel would perform before Shapur Malka with eight cups of wine, throwing one and catching another, without the wine spilling. In Berakhot 56, beginning of side a, Shapur Malka said to Shmuel, “You say that you are very wise. Tell me what I shall see in my dream”; he told him, and so forth. In Mo'ed Katan 26a, Shapur Malka said to Shmuel, “Let it count to my credit that I have never killed a Jew.” Since we find Shapur Malka in Shmuel's time and in Rava's time, as above—see there—and they also said, “Rabbi's stable attendant was wealthier than Shapur Malka,” which suggests that he also lived in Rabbi's time, it therefore appears that all Persian kings were called Shapur Malka, just as Egyptian kings were called Pharaoh.

2. She'erit Yosef, Netiv ha-Perush, interpreter 2, rule 6, writes in Ramban's name that objections may be raised from Shmuel even though he is an amora, because his stature was great; see above, Rav. Rav applied to him, “No secret escapes him”: Ellu Terefot, 59a. Rav and Shmuel (and R' Yohanan) are called kera'ei. Rashi in Megillah explains—this is not there, but in Avodah Zarah—that their words are like Scripture. The Arukh explains it as “lords” in Greek; I did not find this in the Arukh. In Avodah Zarah 40a: “I heard this matter from three kera'ei.” Rashi explains: from three great sages on whom it is fitting to rely as on Scripture. See Rav Hinena bar Idi.

In Hullin 95b, R' Yohanan wrote to Rav, “Before our teacher.” When Rav died he wrote to Shmuel, “Before our colleague.” Shmuel sent him intercalations for twenty-two years (sixty years), but R' Yohanan did not accept him as his teacher, saying, “He knows mere calculation.” Afterward he sent thirteen camels—Tosafot: parchment sheets bearing written queries—of doubtful cases concerning tereifot. He said, “I have a teacher in Babylonia,” and wished to go. He asked a child, “Recite your verse to me,” and the child said, “And Shmuel died.” In the Jerusalem Talmud, at the end of Ba-Meh Ishah, R' Yohanan and R' Shimon ben Lakish wished to go to see Shmuel and heard children saying, “And Shmuel died”; and that was indeed so. But Hullin, there, says: “It was not so; Shmuel had not died. It was only so that he should not trouble himself.” At the end of Mo'ed Katan, 24a, Shmuel rent thirteen garments for Rav. He also rent for one of the rabbis; see Rav Sehorah and Jerusalem Mo'ed Katan, chapter Megallehin, halakhah 7.

In Shemonah Sheratzim, 108a, Rav cursed him, thinking that Shmuel was causing him pain, and his sons did not survive while Rav was alive—only daughters, in the Arukh, the second entry Dal. Rav used to show him honor because he had cursed him: Merubbeh, 80, beginning of side b, and Rashi, Megillah 22, end of side a. Afterward he had sons: Levi, Rav Pappa, Rabbah, and Rami [ורמילא in the witness; provisionally segmented as ורמי followed by לא]. I do not know whence this is derived. His daughters were captured and redeemed, and came before R' Hanina, who permitted them to marry into the priesthood; see below, Shemen bar Abba the priest. Shmuel said, “… and Abba agrees with me ….” Who is Abba? Rav—see his entry—or Abba bar Avahu: Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Bava Kamma. They sent to Shmuel from Rav's academy, “Let our teacher instruct us”: Gittin 66b. R' Shimon son of Rabbi said before him—another reading: R' Yishmael son of R' Yose—…; he said to him, “Be silent, my son”: there, 67a.

3. He was head of the academy in Nehardea: Shabbat 116b and Rashi, Hullin 45b. “He was not in Bavel, but in Nehardea”: Rashi, Megillah 22, end of side a, before Rav went down to Babylonia. See Part I, year 3979. See Yuhasin, letter dalet: “When Rav Dimi went up to Nehardea.” This is difficult to me, for Nehardea is in Babylonia, yet it uses the language of ascent. Perhaps it is because it is on the frontier, as in Mi she-Hotzi'uhu. But in the Arukh, entry Al, it says concerning the first chapter of Ta'anit, 10a, “The upper ones need water; the lower ones do not need water”: Shmuel was in Nehardea and Rav in Sura, and both were on the Euphrates. Nehardea was more than twenty parasangs above Sura. Shmuel and Nehardea needed water; Rav and Sura, which were lower, where the water collected, did not need water. Accordingly, its reading is that Rav said that day sixty is like the time before day sixty, and Shmuel that it is like the time after day sixty. Rashi explained “upper ones” as Rav, who came from the Land of Israel, which is higher, and that Shmuel did not need water because he was from lower Babylonia. He was forced into this by his reading. This is very difficult to me: Rav and Shmuel were both from Babylonia; both went up to the Land of Israel to study with Rabbi—Shmuel was Rabbi's physician—and both went down from the Land of Israel to Babylonia. Shmuel was head of the academy in Nehardea and Rav in Sura; only Shmuel came to Nehardea first. The Arukh's explanation therefore seems preferable. Moreover, the author of the Arukh went to Babylonia and saw with his own eyes that this was so. In Hullin 56a, “When Ze'iri went up to Nehardea,” Rashi explains, “When he went up from Bavel to Nehardea,” in accordance with the Arukh's explanation. End of the quotation from Yuhasin.

He died in the year 4010, six years after Rav. Yuhasin, in Rav Sherira Gaon's name, writes seven years. After Rav's death, his academy came to him, and there was one academy: Yuhasin, there. Sefer Keritut writes that after his death Pappos ben Polemos came and destroyed his great academy, in year 589 of the Era of Documents: Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah 34a. Sefer Keritut writes that the region of Nehardea was at peace for 455 years, until Shmuel's death. Rav Nahman said, “A tanna of Shmuel's academy”: Eruvin 86a. In the Rif, “In Shmuel's academy they taught.” In Beitzah 29, end of side a, Rashi explains “a tanna of Shmuel's academy”: in the Tosefta that Shmuel arranged from tannaim who preceded him, just as R' Hiyya and R' Hoshaya arranged collections, and just as Rabbi arranged the Mishnah. End of quotation.

4. He received from his father and from Levi. He reports in Levi's name: Eruvin 10, end of side a; Sukkah 7, beginning of side a; Nedarim 82a; Menahot 39b. In Berakhot 18, end of side b, Rashi explains that Levi was Shmuel's colleague. Rashbam likewise writes in Arvei Pesahim, 103a, that Rav, Levi, and Shmuel were colleagues. Rambam writes that Shmuel received from R' Hanina bar Hama. Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah 32b writes likewise. In Bekhorot 11b, “R' Shmuel said in R' Hanina's name”: the word R' is a scribal error, since he was not ordained. Raavad objected to him: he did not receive from R' Hanina, but from Levi. This also appears in Shemonah Sheratzim, 108b. It is not proved from there that he did not receive from R' Hanina; there he merely reports in Levi's name. There is some evidence that Shmuel was Levi's pupil: at the beginning of Ha-Tekhelet, there, Levi said to Shmuel, “Aryokh, do not sit down on your feet until you explain to me ….” It would not be proper conduct to say this [to someone who was not his pupil]; see R' Yoshiyah de-Dari.

In Berakhot 18b, orphans' money had been entrusted to Shmuel's father. When he died, Shmuel was not with him. They used to call him “the son of the man who consumes orphans' money.” He went to the court of death and said, “I want Abba.” They told him, “There are many Abbas here.” He said, “I want Abba bar Abba.” They told him, “There are many of those here too.” He said, “I want Abba bar Abba, Shmuel's father.” They told him, “He has gone up to the heavenly academy.” Meanwhile he saw Levi sitting outside, and so forth; see there. Meanwhile his father came. Shmuel saw his father weeping and laughing. He asked him, “Why were you weeping?” He answered, “Because you will come soon”—you will soon be buried. “Why were you laughing?” “Because you are very highly regarded in this world.” He said to him, “If I am highly regarded, let them admit Levi”; and they admitted Levi. He asked him, “Where is the orphans' money?” He said, “In the mill channel. The upper and lower money is ours: if thieves steal it or the earth consumes it, it will be from ours. The middle money belongs to the orphans.” Rambam, in the introduction to the Yad, says that Shmuel belonged to Rabbi's court. Raavad writes that this was not so. In my humble opinion, his evidence appears to be the statement that Shmuel was Rabbi's physician: Maginnei Shelomoh, Hullin 5.

5. (a) The halakhah follows Shmuel in civil law; see above. Rosh gives the reason in chapter 4 of Bava Kamma and in Ha-Zahav. This applies specifically against Rav, not against R' Yohanan. In Eruvin 90b, Rav and Shmuel disagree, and Shmuel himself says that the halakhah follows Rav. Nevertheless, in many laws concerning prohibitions, the halakhah follows Shmuel; see Bekhorot 49b. In Shabbat 22a, Abaye mentioned three laws in which Rabbah followed Shmuel's practice. Some dispute this rule: see Tosafot, Gittin 60b, and Migdal Oz at the end of chapter 7 of Hilkhot Nedarim. Tosafot, Bava Metzia 99, do not accept this rule absolutely. Alternatively, one may say that this rule was stated only where they disagree directly about a law, not through a difference in how they interpret a case; see there and responsa Havvot Ya'ir. In Tosafot, Sukkah 14, end of side b: although the halakhah follows Rav concerning prohibitions, here it follows Shmuel; see Rav. Where Rav and Shmuel disagree about something involving both prohibition and monetary law—see there—Rosh writes in Ha-Megaresh that it is proved that the halakhah follows Rav, since they acted in accordance with Rav in Nehardea. But their following Shmuel in Nehardea is not adduced as proof that the halakhah follows Shmuel, because it was Shmuel's locality; see there, 117, beginning of side a.

(b) Shmuel and R' Yohanan: see his entry. (c) Shmuel and R' Hiyya: the halakhah follows R' Hiyya; Maharik, no. 100. (d) Shmuel and Rav Assi: Asheri, at the end of Kiddushin, rules in accordance with Rav Assi; see his entry. Rashi in Ha-Gozel, 99, rules in accordance with Shmuel against Rav Assi; see his entry. In Bava Kamma they disagree in monetary law, so he rules in accordance with Shmuel, whom the halakhah follows in monetary law. At the end of Kiddushin they disagree concerning prohibitions, so he rules in accordance with Rav Assi, Rav's pupil, since the halakhah follows Rav concerning prohibitions. (e) Shmuel and Rav Adda bar Ahavah: the halakhah follows Shmuel; ה״ע [provisionally Halikhot Olam] 35a. (f) Shmuel and Rav Hisda: the halakhah follows Shmuel; Ran, beginning of Mefannin.

6. In Sefer Gilgulei Neshamot: Aryokh king of Ellasar was reincarnated in Rav and Shmuel, as though it said “Aryokh and king of Ellasar,” with the word “king” expounded both with what precedes and with what follows it. “Aryokh king” is Shmuel, who too is called Aryokh; “king of Ellasar” is Rav, king in matters of prohibition, for the halakhah follows Rav in prohibitions and Shmuel in civil law. Shmuel was a spark of King Shaul, and therefore was called “Aryokh king”; see Abba bar Abba, Shmuel's father. His soul was reincarnated in Rambam; see Part I, year 4865.
Those mentioned as speaking in the name of Shmuel without a further identifying designation:

7. R' Abba; R' Abba bar Zutra; R' Abba bar Yirmeyah. Avit or Ivat bar Ihi, before him. Avin bar Shmuel. He said to Ivat, “Ewe.” Rav Adda bar Ahavah, in his time; R' Ahli, in his time; Rav Illai son of Elazar, in his time. In the name of ראב״צ [provisionally R' Elazar ben Tzadok]; in the name of ראב״ש [provisionally R' Elazar ben Shimon], Ketubbot 44a. R' Elazar ben Pedat, his pupil. Eliezer Ze'ira, in his time. R' Ammi bar Mattana. R' Assi, greater in standing than he. Ben ha-Madori. R' Bannai, or Ravnai, or Yannai. Rav Giddel; Rav Giddel bar Menashi. Rav Dimi bar Yosef; he asked ר״ה [provisionally Rav Huna]—see his entry. Rav Huna or Hana of Baghdad, his pupil. Rav Huna bar Hiyya. Rav Huna bar Yehudah—this requires examination. R' Hila. Zevulun ben Dan.

R' Zeira. In R' Ze'ira's name; in R' Hiyya's name. R' Hiyya bar Avin. R' Hiyya bar Ashi, in his name. He said to R' Hiyya bar Rav, “Torah scholar” [בר אוריין]. R' Hiyya bar Mattana. R' Hiyya bar Yosef. R' Hiyya the merchant, in his time. He said to R' Hiyya bar Rav Idi. He said to Hinena bar Shila. R' Hama ben Gurya, in his time. R' Hanilai bar Idi. R' Hanan bar Ashi. R' Hanina bar Idi. R' Hanina said; see above. In R' Hanina ben Antigonos's name: Hullin 53b; Niddah 5a. Rav Hanan bar Yitzhak. Rav Hanan bar Rava. And R' Hanan bar Ammi. R' Hanan of Gufta, before him. R' Hinena bar Kahana. Hananyah. R' Hisda.

R' Tavit the fowler. Tavi, the grandson of Mari Tavi, in his time. R' Tavi. R' Tuvi bar Kisna. R' Yoshiyah of Usha, in his name. Rav Yehudah. Mar Yohani asked him. R' Yohanan asked him: Mo'ed Katan 24, beginning of side a. Rav Yosef bar Menashya. R' Yannai bar Nahmani. R' Yitzhak bar Bisna. R' Yitzhak bar Nahman. R' Yirmeyah. He said to R' Yirmeyah of Shavshav. R' Yirmeyah bar Abba said in Shmuel's name. In R' Yishmael's name: Yevamot 96b; Ketubbot 51b, 57b, 74a; Niddah 22, end of side b; Nedarim 74. R' Yishmael son of R' Yose; see above.

Rav Kahana bar Hinena. Rav Kahana bar Yirmeyah. Levi, his teacher or colleague; see above. Levi, his son. Luda, in his time. Rav Muna—requires examination. R' Menashya of Dvil. Mar bar ha-Madori, before him. Mari bar Mar, in his time. Mari bar Mar Ukva. R' Mattana. Mattityahu bar Yehudah. Nehorai. R' Nehalai bar Idi. Rav Nahman bar Yaakov. Rav Nahman bar Adda. Nittai. R' Natan, before him. R' Natan bar Hoshaya. Mar Ukva; see his entry. Ukva bar Nehemyah, the exilarch. Rav Anan. Rav Anan bar Tahlifa, before him. R' Anan bar Hiyya. Bar Piyoli, before him. In Paltiah of Naveh's name. R' Pinhas, his brother. Rav Pappa, his son. Karnai, his colleague. He asked Rav: Ketubbot 22, end of side a.

Rava said in Shmuel's name. Rabbah, his son. Rabbah bar Yirmeyah: Rabbah in his name, Menahot 39a, and Zevahim 39 in the new Talmud editions [שס״ח; specific edition and compressed reporting syntax uncollated]. Rabbah bar Rav Huna. רבב״ח [provisionally Rabbah bar bar Hana]. Rabbah bar Hiyya Ketosfa’ah [קטוספאה; epithet interpretation unresolved]. “Our masters in Babylonia”: Rav and Shmuel. Ravnai. Rami, his son. Rami bar Dekula. In Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam's name. Rav Shishi bar Rav Idi, in R' Shimon ben Elazar's name. In Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's name. R' Shimon son of Rabbi; see above. R' Tahlifa bar Avdimi.
